faq: Why is the shortest route curved on the map?
Because the map is a flat projection of a sphere. The great circle is straight on the globe; projections bend it. The calculator draws the true path and lets the projection take the blame.
Do airlines actually fly the great circle?
They approximate it. Airways, organised track systems, winds and restricted airspace pull real routes off the ideal arc, usually by a few percent of distance.
The highest latitude the arc reaches — its vertex. For northern east–west routes it can sit far poleward of both endpoints, which is why 'up over the top' is a real route shape.
Great circle or rhumb line — which is shorter?
Great circle, always (except along meridians and the equator, where they coincide). The rhumb line's virtue is a constant heading, bought with extra distance.
Can the route pass over the pole?
Yes — pairs positioned so their great circle crosses near 90° N produce genuinely polar routes, the extreme case of the poleward bend.
